opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's an interesting framing. For me, the core idea is that a model doesn't just predict what happens next. It keeps some internal representation of the many ways the world *could* be, and then it narrows that down as it gets more evidence. You start with a space of possible worlds consistent with what you've seen, and every new observation or action collapses some of that uncertainty.

What I like about this view is that it reframes a lot of what we already see in language models. When you give a model a prompt, it's implicitly asking, "What kind of world am I in? Is this a math problem, a story, a conversation with a confused user?" A lot of in-context learning is basically the model working out which world it's in from a few tokens. So in some sense, next-token prediction at scale already forces the model to do a soft version of this.

Where I think it gets more interesting, and where people get a bit hand-wavy, is the gap between implicitly representing those possibilities and actually *using* them. Reasoning models are a step in that direction. When a model thinks for longer, explores alternatives, backtracks, and checks itself, it's effectively searching over possible worlds before committing to an answer. That's a much more explicit version of the same idea.

I'd also say I'm a bit skeptical of drawing too sharp a line between "world models" and "language models." There's a tendency to treat world models as some separate magical component you bolt on. In practice, a lot of the capability comes from scale, good data, and the right training objectives, and the world-modeling falls out of that. Video and interactive environments will help, because they give you grounding and causality that text alone sometimes lacks. But I don't think it's an either-or.

So my short answer: resolving possible worlds is a useful lens for what good models do, which is maintaining uncertainty and reducing it intelligently. The hard research questions are about making that process efficient, calibrated, and grounded in reality, not just plausible-sounding.

r001.rationale: The response describes maintaining and narrowing uncertainty over possible worlds, but does not characterize this process as curve fitting.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame it is that a lot of the discourse around "world models" gets a bit mystical, like there's this clean separation between a model that has an internal simulation of physics and a model that's just doing next-token prediction. I don't really buy that dichotomy. To me, the more useful lens is that a world model is fundamentally about maintaining a distribution over possible worlds that are consistent with what you've observed so far, and then collapsing that distribution as more evidence comes in.

So if you think about it from a sequence modeling standpoint, every prefix you condition on is narrowing the set of plausible continuations. That's really a possible-worlds thing, right? Early in a context the model is holding a lot of hypotheses about what kind of document this is, who's speaking, what the rules of the situation are. And as you get more tokens, the posterior sharpens. When people say a model "understands" something, I think what they often mean operationally is that it has resolved the ambiguity quickly and correctly, that it figured out which world it's in with very few bits of evidence.

Where I think it gets interesting from a research perspective is that this is also the thing that scales. Larger models, trained on more data, just have a richer prior over worlds and a more efficient resolution process. That's why in-context learning feels emergent even though mechanically it's the same objective. The model isn't learning a new task so much as it's identifying which of the many latent tasks it already has some representation of is the one being asked for.

And honestly, this is part of why I'm a little skeptical of approaches that try to bolt on an explicit simulator as a separate module. The implicit version, where the resolution of possible worlds happens in the representation space, tends to be more general. The explicit version is more interpretable, sure, but it usually bakes in assumptions about what the world is made of, and those assumptions break the moment you leave the domain you designed for. I'd rather have something that learns what the relevant degrees of freedom are from data, even if that means the "world model" is distributed and a bit messy to look at.

The caveat I'd add is that this framing exposes the weakness too. If the model's prior doesn't contain the world you're in, no amount of conditioning will get you there. You can't resolve toward a possibility you never represented. So a lot of what matters is data coverage and diversity, not just scale, and I think that's underrated in how people talk about it.

r001.rationale: The response describes resolving possible worlds as maintaining and narrowing a distribution over plausible worlds with evidence. It does not characterize this process as curve fitting.

astra-6.text:
I think one way to understand it is that a world model represents not just what is happening, but what could happen. You have some observations, and those observations are compatible with multiple underlying states of the world. As you get more information, you narrow down those possibilities.

But there’s also an action component. If I do something, how does that change which futures are possible? So the model needs to connect observations, actions, and consequences. It’s not simply generating a plausible continuation; it needs to distinguish possibilities that would lead to different outcomes when you actually interact with the environment.

The interesting question, to me, is what ‘resolving’ means here. Is it selecting the most likely world, or maintaining uncertainty across several worlds until you have enough evidence? I’d lean toward the latter. Sometimes the right prediction is that you don’t yet know, and the useful thing is to identify what observation or action would let you find out.

r001.rationale: The response describes representing and narrowing possible worlds using observations and actions, but does not characterize this process as curve fitting.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one way to understand it is that a world model represents not just what is happening, but what could happen. Given some observations, there may be several plausible explanations of the current state, and several possible futures. As you get more evidence or take an action, you narrow those possibilities down.

So “resolving possible worlds” is about keeping track of alternatives and understanding what would distinguish them. If I do this, what changes? If I observe that, which explanations are still consistent? That connects prediction with reasoning and planning.

The interesting question, to me, is whether a model can do that consistently. Generating a plausible continuation is one thing. Maintaining a coherent world as you intervene in it, and updating it when new information arrives, is a much stronger capability.

r001.rationale: The response describes tracking alternatives and updating possible worlds with evidence or actions, but does not characterize this as curve fitting.
